📄 Iran’s security chief: Basij force is a major national asset

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) Major General Mohsen Rezaei has described Iran’s Basij force as a major national asset, saying its roots in the country’s history, culture, faith and public participation give it a distinction few nations possess.

In a message marking Basij Week, Rezaei said on Thursday that the Basij Organization was among the most enduring initiatives of the late Imam Khomeini and one of Iran’s greatest national resources.
​
He recalled that the order to establish the Basij was issued on November 26, 1979, adding that the initiative had demonstrated that a nation’s strength depends not only on military forces, equipment and material resources, but also on faith, determination, knowledge and preparedness.
​
Many countries possess economic and military power, but having such an extensive asset, rooted in history, culture, faith and public participation, is a rare advantage, he said.
​
Rezaei said the Basij’s role should be viewed beyond defense, encompassing national security, strength, science and technology, the economy, production, development and poverty alleviation.
​
He added that building a powerful Iran with global influence requires more than military capabilities, stressing the importance of human resources, national determination, knowledge and public responsibility, adding that Basij is one of the main pillars of this national power.
​
Rezaei concluded by marking Basij Week and paying tribute to its members and those serving the Iranian people.

78. The Carnation Revolution

The Carnation Revolution of April 1974 is remembered as a peaceful and symbolic political transition, marked by flowers in rifle barrels and soldiers in the arms of civilians. However, beneath the surface lay decades of extensive state overreach, cultural repression and individual hardship. The Portuguese dictatorship extended its control beyond institutions, seeking to dominate language, art, collective memory and emotional expression. In that environment, music became one of the few remaining spaces where truth could survive. José “Zeca” Afonso emerged as one of the most significant figures in this cultural resistance, not because he sought political power, but because his voice reached people in a way the regime could not silence.

The Estado Novo (New State) regime exercised widespread control over Portuguese society. Censorship boards reviewed every song, poem, newspaper article and performance. Lyrics were subject to modification or prohibition, artists were blacklisted and radio stations were rigorously monitored. The secret police maintained detailed files on musicians and writers, surveilled their movements, interrogated their associates and detained individuals deemed politically subversive. It entered homes, schools and workplaces and it shaped what people were allowed to say, sing, read and even imagine.

Zeca Afonso lived directly under this pressure. His songs were frequently censored, his performances were disrupted and his income was restricted through professional exclusion. He was arrested multiple times, imprisoned and subjected to harsh interrogation and torture. These experiences were not incidental to his art. They informed it. Afonso wrote from the position of someone who had personally encountered the violence of the state. His music carried the voice of prisoners, laborers, rural communities and the politically silenced. His calm, restrained delivery stood in stark contrast to the brutality behind the walls that confined him.

Rather than producing explicit slogans, Afonso embedded resistance within folk forms familiar to ordinary people, many illiterate by design. His songs spoke of brotherhood, equality, shared labour and dignity. This allowed them to circulate quietly between friends, to be sung at gatherings and be remembered when recordings were confiscated. Music became a form of memory storage and emotional continuity. Some crossed the border to Spain to obtain his records to play clandestinely. His music preserved an alternative moral order when the official one had become coercive and suppressive.

Red carnations remain an emblem of Portugal. They were not planned as a symbol by generals or politicians. They were offered by ordinary people, including a florist who handed the flowers to soldiers with unloaded rifles. The gesture transformed the atmosphere of the uprising. It redefined the meaning of force. Weapons were present, but they were rendered inert by military refusal to turn them against the people. The revolution became a public act, not only a military one.

This is why the song "Grândola, Vila Morena" mattered so deeply. Over 50 years later, it still does. It is sung a cappella to the sound of the marching boots of the people. It was played at midnight on the radio to signal the beginning of the revolution. It did not announce a leader. It announced a people. It named fraternity as the foundation of political life. That message resonated because people had lived under surveillance, suspicion, enforced silence and fear. 

The relevance of this story does not end in 1974. The Carnation Revolution invites reflection on how much power governments should hold over speech, movement, employment and cultural life. The Portuguese case suggests that any authority can become dangerous when it is unaccountable, centralised and insulated from consequences. The legacy of Afonso raises a question that remains open: how much freedom must be surrendered before a society forgets what freedom feels like and how many songs does it take to remind people again?
